chapter.title: Three checks in five minutes

cards.body:
Two companies own the same £10 million of stuff and make the same £1 million profit. One is a safe bet and one is a gamble, and **three quick sums** on the balance sheet tell you which.

In house terms, you check three things. Do this month's bills fit inside the current account? How much of the house does the bank really own? Does the cash on the kitchen table cover the loan due soon?
cards.simpler: Picture two companies. Each owns £10 million of stuff and makes £1 million profit. Yet one is a safe bet and the other is a gamble. **Three quick sums** on the balance sheet show you which is which. Think of it like checking a house. Do this month's bills fit inside the current account? How much of the house does the bank really own? Does the cash on the kitchen table cover the loan due soon?

cards.prompt: Priya owns a £300,000 house. Her current account holds £3,000. This month she owes £4,500 in bills, including a £2,000 loan repayment. Can she pay this month without selling anything or borrowing?

options.text: Yes, easily: she owns a £300,000 house.
No: £3,000 in the account can't cover £4,500 due now.
Can't say without knowing her salary last year.

whyNot.a: That's what she owns, not what she can spend this month: you can't pay the electricity bill with a bedroom.
whyNot.c: That's last year's film, not today's photo: the question is about the money and the bills on the table now.

cards.reteach: Owning a lot doesn't pay small bills. This month, what counts is the money that can move this month, set against what's due this month. Compare those two and leave the house out of it.

cards.title: Three pairs of lines
cards.body:
Each check is just two lines from the sheet, side by side. **Pick the right pair and the sum does the rest.**

Check one: *current assets* (things that turn into cash within 12 months) against *current liabilities* (bills due within 12 months). Divide the first by the second. Below 1.0 means more is due this year than is coming in. That's Priya's kitchen table.

Check two: everything the company owes against its equity, the owners' share. It shows how much of the house the bank owns.

Check three: plain cash against short-term loans. No stock, no unpaid customer bills. Just money in the drawer.
cards.simpler: Each check puts two lines from the sheet side by side. **Pick the right pair and the sum does the rest.** Check one divides current assets (things that turn into cash within a year) by current liabilities (bills due within a year). Below 1.0, more is due than is coming in. That's Priya's kitchen table. Check two weighs all debts against equity, the owners' share. Check three weighs plain cash against short-term loans. It's just the money in the drawer.

cards.title: Kettle and Brew
cards.body:
Two coffee roasters each own £10m of assets and make £1m profit. Kettle has £4m of current assets against £2m due this year, a ratio of 2.0. It owes £4m in total against £6m of equity, and holds £1.5m of cash against £0.5m of loans due. Brew has the same £4m against £5m due (0.8) and owes £8m against just £2m of equity. **It has £200,000 in the bank and a £3m loan due before next Christmas.**

Same profit. Very different Christmas.
cards.simpler: Two coffee roasters each own £10m and make £1m profit. Kettle has £4m of current assets against £2m due this year, a ratio of 2.0. It owes £4m against £6m of equity and holds £1.5m cash against £0.5m of loans due. Brew has the same £4m against £5m due, just 0.8, and owes £8m against £2m of equity. **It has £200,000 in the bank and a £3m loan due before next Christmas.** Same profit. Very different Christmas.

cards.prompt: Lumen Lamps, 31 March: current assets £600,000, current liabilities £400,000, cash £50,000, short-term loans £300,000. Which reading is right?

options.text: Healthy: current assets beat current liabilities, so it can pay this year.
Passes check one at 1.5, fails check three: £50,000 of cash against £300,000 of loans due.
Fails check one: £400,000 of bills is too many.

whyNot.a: That's check one on its own. Check three, cash against loans, tells a different story.
whyNot.c: That's reading one line, not a pair: £400,000 due is fine when £600,000 is coming in.

cards.reteach: Run all three pairs, not just the first. Lumen's 1.5 says enough is coming in this year, but only £50,000 of it is actual cash. The rest is lamps on shelves and customer bills that may not be paid in time.

cards.title: What good looks like
cards.body:
Check one: above 1.5 is comfortable, and below 1.0 needs a reason. Benjamin Graham, who wrote the classic line-by-line guide to these sheets, liked to see about 2 to 1.

Check two: owing less than the equity is calm. Owing four times as much, like Brew, means one bad year can wipe the owners out. If equity is negative, skip the sum. That's already your answer.

You'd think a low check one is always bad. It isn't. Supermarkets often run below 1.0, because shoppers pay at the till today and suppliers get paid weeks later. **Compare a company with its own trade.**
cards.simpler: Check one: above 1.5 is comfortable, and below 1.0 needs a reason. Benjamin Graham, author of the classic guide, liked about 2 to 1. Check two: owing less than equity is calm. Owing four times as much, like Brew, means one bad year can wipe out the owners. Negative equity is your answer. A low check one isn't always bad. Supermarkets often sit below 1.0, since shoppers pay today but suppliers get paid weeks later. **Compare a company with its own trade.**

cards.body: Tom runs check one on a toy shop in October, gets 2.2 and calls it safe. But £1.8m of its £2m in current assets is unsold toys and unpaid customer bills, and the cash would fit in a shoebox. To spot this, run check three straight after check one. If the ratio looks great but cash is tiny, **the good number is made of stuff, not money**.
cards.simpler: Tom checks a toy shop in October. Check one gives 2.2, so he calls it safe. But £1.8m of its £2m in current assets is unsold toys and bills customers haven't paid yet. The actual cash would fit in a shoebox. So run check three right after check one. If the ratio looks great but the cash is tiny, **the good number is made of stuff, not money**.

cards.prompt: A bank wants to know one thing: can this company repay the loans due this year without selling stock or borrowing again? Which pair of lines answers that?

whyNot.a: That's check one, the wider net: it counts stock and customer bills that might not turn into cash in time.
whyNot.c: That's check two: it measures how much is borrowed overall, not what's due this year.

cards.reteach: Each check answers a different question. Check one asks whether enough will come in this year. Check two asks how much of the house the bank owns. Check three asks whether there's money in the drawer right now for the loans due soon, and it's the only one that ignores stock and unpaid bills.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Three pairs of lines tell you whether a company can pay its way: current assets against current liabilities, everything owed against equity, and cash against loans due this year. **Run all three**, because one good number can hide a bad one.

Tomorrow: why last year's column is the most useful one on the page.
cards.simpler: Three pairs of lines tell you if a company can pay its way. Current assets against current liabilities. Everything owed against equity. Cash against loans due this year. **Run all three**, because one good number can hide a bad one, like a tidy front room hiding a leaking roof. Tomorrow: why last year's column is the most useful one on the page.

cards.body: Look up the latest annual report of a listed company you bought from this week. Find the balance sheet and divide current assets by current liabilities. Is it above or below 1.0?
cards.simpler: Pick a listed company, one whose shares anyone can buy, that you bought something from this week. Find its latest annual report and turn to the balance sheet. **Divide current assets by current liabilities.** This is check one. Is the answer above or below 1.0?

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now run three quick checks on a balance sheet and say whether a company can pay its bills this year.
